title: What Gear Is Essential for Trail Running?
excerpt: Trail running kit by how far and how remote you run: shoes, hydration, layers, a light and safety gear, including which satellite messengers are two-way.
body:
What Gear Is Essential for Trail Running?

Updated November 2026. Prices are US list prices (MSRP) at the time of this update; retailers often sell for less.

The gear you need for trail running depends on two things: how long you'll be out and how far you'll be from help. A one-hour loop on a busy local trail needs little more than trail shoes and water. A remote mountain run needs layers, a light, food and a way to call for help. This guide goes from the essentials to the safety kit. It's based on manufacturer specs and published reviews. We haven't tested these products ourselves.

Safety: know whether your messenger is one-way or two-way

Beyond phone signal, a satellite device is the only way to call for help. These devices are not all the same:

  • Two-way messengers, such as the Garmin inReach Mini 2 (about 100 g), let you send messages and receive replies, and trigger an SOS. You can confirm that help is coming and answer rescuers' questions.
  • One-way messengers, such as the SPOT Gen4, can send your location, preset check-in messages and an SOS, but cannot receive replies. You won't know whether a message got through or whether help is on the way.

Both types need a subscription. For remote solo runs, choose a two-way device. Whichever you carry, tell someone your route and expected return time.

Shoes

Trail shoes differ from road shoes mainly in grip, underfoot protection and upper durability. Choose lug depth to suit your terrain:

  • Gentle, hard-packed trails: a cushioned shoe with modest lugs, such as the Hoka Challenger 8.
  • Mixed and technical terrain: the Hoka Speedgoat 7, with lugs of about 5 mm.
  • Mud and soft ground: deeper, more widely spaced lugs, such as on the Salomon Speedcross 6.

On long descents your foot slides forward, so leave some room at the toe.

Hydration

  • Under about an hour, on familiar trails: a handheld soft flask or a waist belt.
  • Longer runs, or anywhere remote: a running vest with front flasks. It also gives you room for food, a layer and safety kit.

Plan your water around where you can refill, not just distance. Hot weather and long climbs raise how much you need.

Clothing

  • Moisture-wicking base layers (synthetic or merino) rather than cotton.
  • A light windproof or waterproof jacket for anything exposed, even when the forecast looks fine.
  • A warm layer, a hat and gloves for mountain or cold-weather runs.
  • Trail socks that fit well. Toe socks help some runners avoid blisters between toes.

Light, navigation and sun

  • Headlamp: carry one on any run that could finish near dusk. Brighter, wider beams make technical ground easier to see.
  • Navigation: load the route on your phone or watch, and know how to use it. Among watches, the Garmin Forerunner 970 has offline maps. The Suunto Vertical 2 is rated for 65 hours of dual-band GPS. The Garmin Forerunner 170 is a cheaper option for tracking without maps.
  • Sun: UV exposure increases with altitude, so wear sunglasses and sunscreen on high, exposed runs.

Emergency kit for remote runs

  • An emergency blanket or bivvy
  • A whistle
  • A small first-aid kit (blister care, tape, bandage)
  • Spare food
  • A charged phone, plus a satellite messenger beyond signal (see above)

Trekking poles

Poles help on long, steep climbs and descents, and some mountain races allow or recommend them. On rolling or runnable trails they mostly get in the way. Practise with them before race day.

Build your kit by stage

  • Starting out: trail shoes, a handheld flask, a light jacket and a phone.
  • Longer runs: add a vest, food, a headlamp and a basic first-aid kit.
  • Remote and mountain runs: add warm layers, an emergency bivvy, navigation, and a two-way satellite messenger if you'll be out of signal.

keyTakeaway: Match your kit to how remote the run is, not just how long: on short local loops you need shoes and water; far from help you need layers, a light and a way to call for help.
